title: Numbers 14:1–10
context: The congregation weeps through the night and grumbles against Moses and Aaron, wishing they had died in Egypt and proposing a new leader to take them back. Moses and Aaron fall on their faces. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead that the land is good and that the LORD is with Israel, but the people threaten to stone them until the LORD’s glory appears.

verses.text: All the congregation lifted up their voice, and cried; and the people wept that night.
verses.arminianNotes: The whole congregation weeps all night. The spies’ report has spread despair through the nation. Arminian readers note how the unbelief of leaders shapes the response of a people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same corporate collapse. Fear spreads when God’s promise is set aside. This is shared ground.

verses.text: All the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron. The whole congregation said to them, “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt, or that we had died in this wilderness!
verses.arminianNotes: The people grumble against Moses and Aaron and wish they had died in Egypt or in the wilderness. The wish is grimly answered in verses 28–29. Grumbling against God’s appointed leaders is grumbling against God himself (compare Exodus 16:8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers draw the same connection. The words of unbelief become the terms of judgment. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Why does the LORD bring us to this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our little ones will be captured or killed! Wouldn’t it be better for us to return into Egypt?”
verses.arminianNotes: The people accuse the LORD of bringing them to die by the sword and fear for their wives and children. They suggest returning to Egypt. They interpret God’s purposes in the worst possible light.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see here the heart of unbelief: suspecting God’s goodness. Ironically, the children they claim to protect are the ones God will bring into the land (verse 31). This is shared ground.

verses.text: They said to one another, “Let’s choose a leader, and let’s return into Egypt.”
verses.arminianNotes: They propose choosing a leader to go back to Egypt. This is a rejection of Moses and, through him, of God’s redemption from slavery.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read this as covenant rebellion: turning back from the God who saved them. Both traditions see the proposal as a reversal of the exodus.

verses.text: Then Moses and Aaron fell on their faces before all the assembly of the congregation of the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the assembly. The gesture expresses grief, humility, and perhaps intercession. They do not defend themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see humility and appeal to God in this posture. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who were of those who spied out the land, tore their clothes.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes, a sign of mourning and alarm. They alone of the spies stand against the people’s rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same contrast. A faithful minority grieves over the majority’s sin. This is shared ground.

verses.text: They spoke to all the congregation of the children of Israel, saying, “The land, which we passed through to spy it out, is an exceedingly good land.
verses.arminianNotes: They insist the land is “an exceedingly good land.” They answer the evil report with the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Faith speaks accurately about God’s gifts. This is shared ground.

verses.text: If the LORD delights in us, then he will bring us into this land, and give it to us: a land which flows with milk and honey.
verses.arminianNotes: “If the LORD delights in us, then he will bring us into this land.” Their confidence rests on God’s favor and power, not Israel’s strength. Arminian readers note that the condition calls Israel to respond rightly in order to remain in the place of God’s favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the confidence rests on God’s delight and promise. They read the condition as a summons to faith, not as a doubt about God’s faithfulness. Both traditions see faith’s logic here.

verses.text: Only don’t rebel against the LORD, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and the LORD is with us. Don’t fear them.”
verses.arminianNotes: They warn against rebellion and fear: the people of the land are “bread for us,” their protection is gone, and “the LORD is with us.” God’s presence is the decisive fact.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the presence of God as the ground of courage. This is shared ground.

verses.text: But all the congregation threatened to stone them with stones. The LORD’s glory appeared in the Tent of Meeting to all the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The people threaten to stone Joshua and Caleb, but the LORD’s glory appears at the Tent of Meeting. God intervenes to protect his faithful servants and to confront the rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the appearance of glory as both protection and judgment. This is shared ground.
